title: ASIRT clears officers who shot and killed armed suspected drug dealer
article: Alberta's police watchdog has cleared three Edmonton officers of wrongdoing in the 2017 shooting death of a suspected drug trafficker.

Police and the 30-year-old suspect exchanged gunfire during a dramatic takedown attempt outside the Westmount mall McDonald's on Sept. 9, 2017. Two 18-year-old women riding in the man's Mercedes were removed by police as the gunfire ensued.
Reporters at the scene counted at least nine bullet holes in the car's windshield. The deceased fired two shots into the vehicle's dashboard.
During a news conference Monday, Alberta Serious Incident Response Team (ASIRT) executive director Susan Hughson said the officers' use of force was justified.
ASIRT as a policy does not release the names of victims, or, as it calls them, "affected persons." Subsequent media reports identified the deceased as Matt Dumas.
Hughson attributed the violent outcome in part to the methamphetamine coursing through Dumas's body. She also expressed regret over the amount of time it took for ASIRT to conclude its investigation.

"The delay in this particular case is too long," she said. "It's too long for the family of this man, and it's too long for the involved officers. But I think they all recognize the challenges ASIRT is facing."
An ASIRT news release said police had been investigating Dumas for methamphetamine trafficking and planned to raid his home after obtaining a search warrant on Sept. 8, 2017.
Investigators believed Dumas had guns in his possession and decided it would be safest to arrest him while he was in his car or on foot. Hughson said Dumas had a history of fleeing police.

Though Dumas was under police surveillance, the trail went cold until 8 p.m. the following day, when he and two young women were spotted getting behind the wheel of a white Mercedes sedan. Dumas carried a black satchel which police feared contained a firearm.

Unmarked police cars followed the vehicle to the parking lot of Westmount Centre mall. As Dumas backed into a parking stall between a McDonald's and a Boston Pizza, police made the call to box the vehicle in and arrest him.

The scene was immediate chaos. Tactical officers exited the vehicles and deployed two flash-bang grenades to disorient the vehicle's occupants. Dumas and the two women were ordered to show their hands and exit the vehicle. While they initially complied, they refused to leave the car.

Dumas then shook his head, dropped his hands and threw the Mercedes into reverse, ramming a police truck parked behind the vehicle. The sedan then lurched forward, striking a second police vehicle. Officers threw two cans of tear gas into the Mercedes through a passenger-side window.
An instant later, police called for the women to exit the vehicle and one officer began to extricate a woman seated in the front seat. At that point, Dumas reached into the black bag.

One officer yelled "don't do it," while another fired a round from an ARWEN, a launcher that fires a non-lethal projectile made of hard plastic. The shot failed to disarm Dumas, who raised a handgun and pointed it at the nearest officer.
That officer and two others opened fire.
Hughson said, at some point, Dumas fired two rounds into the dash of the Mercedes. He tried to raise his gun again when one of the officers fired the lethal shot.

Paramedics ruled Dumas dead at the scene. The two women in the car were uninjured. Hughson said the two were interviewed as part of the investigation but called them "less than cooperative." All three officers provided statements and notes to ASIRT despite not being required to do so.
Hughson said video footage of the incident was "extremely limited," noting Edmonton officers do not wear body cameras.

Meth played an outsized role in the case's tragic outcome, Hughson said. A subsequent toxicology examination found methamphetamine in Dumas's body. The black satchel he carried contained a "significant" quantity of methamphetamine, a scale, and a second magazine for the 9-mm handgun
"Methamphetamine is our Number 1 problem," Hughson said, noting the drug is "almost always" involved in use of force cases.

"It is one of those drugs that causes impulsive and irrational decisions, and that appears to be part of what took place in this case. If the person was thinking rationally, in my opinion, he would have recognized the overwhelming force and surrendered."
In the aftermath of the shooting, friends of Dumas described him as a "nice, decent guy" whose life took a turn for the worse after his fraternal twin brother killed himself in 2011.
Another friend called him an "open door" kind of guy who struggled with substance abuse issues.
Hughson said the case will likely be the subject of a fatality inquiry, which can result in recommendations to prevent similar deaths.

ASIRT was created in 2008 to investigate allegations of wrongdoing against Alberta police officers. Since then, it has recommended charges against 36 law enforcement members and investigated more than 120 police-involved deaths.
Last year was the agency's busiest on record, with 75 files tied to 68 investigations.
